31.0.0.en: 1 Wakefulness for the sake of riches wastes away the body, and anxiety over it drives away sleep. 2 The wakefulness of anxiety deprives one of slumber, and severe illness is driven off by sleep. 3 The rich man toils in gathering money, and in his rest is filled with delights; 4 the poor man toils for the need of living, and in his rest becomes needy. 5 He who loves gold shall not be justified, and he who follows corruption shall be filled with it. 6 Many have fallen for the sake of gold, and their destruction has come to be before their faces. 7 Gold is a stumblingblock to those who sacrifice to it, and every fool is caught by it. 8 Blessed is the rich man who is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold. 9 Who is he, that we may call him blessed? For he has done wonders among his people. 10 Who has been tried by it and found perfect? Let him glory in it. Who has been able to transgress and has not transgressed, and to do evil and has not done it? 11 His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare his alms. 12 If you sit at a bountiful table, do not open your throat wide over it, 13 and do not say, How much there is upon it!

31.0.1.en: He speaks of the sound use of wealth immediately after speaking of bodily health, because some destroy their health by excessive effort for the sake of wealth. The love of money has gained mastery over many, and has made some careless of the safety of their souls and bodies. Because of the love of money, some are exposed to the following:

31.1.0.en: a. The ruin of bodily health through wakefulness out of love for money [2].

31.1.1.en: b. Suffering from anxiety and being deprived of enough time for sleep [1].

31.2.0.en: c. Some are exposed to bodily illnesses because of luxury and excess in eating [3].

31.3.0.en: d. The love of money drives God's righteousness out of the heart [5], so that a man loses the blessed life and the money itself [8].

31.4.0.en: e. He falls into temptations whenever tribulation comes [10].

31.4.1.en: f. He loses his role in supporting the needy in the holy congregation (the Church).

31.4.2.en: Wakefulness (sleeplessness) for the sake of wealth wastes away the body, and anxiety over wealth drives away sleep [1].

31.4.3.en: Wealth in itself is not evil, but it is a burden to the soul that clings to it, causing it to lose its life and tearing it away from its attachment to its Savior. St. John Chrysostom speaks to us of sleep as a gift of God which He gave us by nature for our rest. But we have no pity on ourselves; rather we stand in enmity with ourselves, inventing for ourselves a tyrant stronger than the force of nature, which robs us of the rest of sleep.

31.4.4.en: * It is said: "Anxiety over wealth drives away sleep" [1]. Behold the greatness of God's providence! He did not leave us the choice to sleep according to our own will, nor according to our need for sleep, but bound us by the necessities of nature, so that what is good for us might come to pass even without our will. To sleep is a matter of nature. But we, like cruel haters of ourselves, like strange enemies and persecutors, invent a tyrant stronger than this necessity of nature, the one that comes from money [1].

31.4.5.en: * Worse than every burning is what comes upon our souls through the bitterness of grief. Just as the body dries up and is wearied by its struggle against the violence of the sun's rays, and is brought into a shelter in which there are several springs, to be calmed by the gentle breeze, so the night does for us, when our souls are given over to sleep. Indeed, I ought rather to say that it is neither the night nor sleep that does this, but God, who knows how great is the toil and misery of our race. Yet we have no mercy on ourselves, as if we were enemies of our own souls, and we gave ourselves a despot stronger than the natural need for sleep, namely sleeplessness because of wealth... Behold the greatness of God's care. For He did not leave the right to rest to our will, nor the need for sleep to our choice, but bound sleep to the necessity of nature, so that we may practice what is good even without our will [2].

31.4.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * When one of the passions of your soul rises up in you, remember that those who think rightly and wish to establish what they have upon a sound and firm foundation do not rejoice in corruptible riches, but in the true glory which is in the heavens, and by this they become blessed. For wealth may be plundered or stolen by those who have greater power, but the virtue of the spirit alone is the faithful possession that cannot be taken away, besides that it rescues its owner after death.

31.4.7.en: Those who think thus are not deceived by the glitter of vain riches and the other delights [3].

31.4.8.en: St. Anthony the Great The care of sleeplessness deprives one of slumber, and severe illness puts an end to sleep [2].

31.4.9.en: One of the accumulated troubles of preoccupation with wealth is that anxiety invades the soul and one suffers from sleeplessness, which also causes bodily illnesses. In this the Apostle Paul says: "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1 Tim 6:9-10).

31.4.10.en: * Why do you envy the rich man? Is it because he has subjected himself to many cares?... For he is bound like a dog with myriads of chains, that is, his wealth!... And it is as though, in a spirit of enmity toward ourselves, we hand ourselves over to a tyrant stronger than the natural need for rest, that is, the sleeplessness that arises from wealth.

31.4.11.en: St. John Chrysostom The rich man toils in gathering money, and in his rest is filled with his luxury [3].

31.4.12.en: St. Ambrose comments thus on the parable of "Lazarus and the rich man" (Lk 16:19-31): [Not every poverty is necessarily holy, nor is every wealth hateful [4].] In other words, poverty is not an end in itself, nor is wealth evil in itself; rather it is the life of man that corrupts the one or the other. The pampered, luxurious life that has no pity on the needy dishonors wealth, and the holy, thankful life adorns poverty.

31.4.13.en: The poor man toils for the need of living, and in his rest becomes needy [4].

31.4.14.en: He who is born in poverty is not to blame for his poverty. If he offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God for the faculties He has given him, then although he is in need in temporal things, he is counted rich in his offerings. This is like the widow who offered two mites (Mk 12:42).

31.4.15.en: He who loves gold is not called righteous, and he who follows the track of gain goes astray because of it [5].

31.4.16.en: St. Cyril the Great comments on the saying of the Lord Christ: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores" (Lk 16:19-31), saying: [I ask you to observe closely the words of the Savior... He called him "rich" simply so, but the poor man He pointed out by name. What do we conclude from this? That the rich man, being unmerciful, was without a name in the presence of God, since it is said elsewhere by the voice of the Psalmist concerning those who do not fear the Lord: "I will not take up their names into my lips" (Ps 16:4); but the poor man, as I said, had his name mentioned by the tongue of God [5].]

31.4.17.en: Many have fallen into disaster for the sake of gold, and their destruction has come to be before their faces [6].

31.4.18.en: * In the parable of Lazarus and the rich man (Lk 16:19-31), in the end the rich man became a beggar asking of the poor man, and begging from the table of him who had been hungry and cast down to the mouths of the dogs. The situation was reversed, and each one came to know who was truly rich and who was truly poor, for Lazarus appeared richer than all, and the other poorer than all.

31.4.19.en: As in the theaters the actors put on the masks of kings, generals, physicians, teachers, professors and soldiers, yet in their reality they are not so, so wealth and poverty here are mere masks. If you sit in a theater and see a man wearing the mask of a king, do not envy him, nor consider that he has become a king, nor desire to be like him... So the rich man here is often poor (in his depths): if you take off his mask, and uncover his conscience, and enter into his thought, you will often find in him the poverty of virtue, and find him belonging to the lowest classes [6].

31.4.20.en: St. John Chrysostom * Hear how the rich man boasted and was glad, he at whose door (Lazarus) was cast down and laid.

31.4.21.en: His body was sound and he was rich in his possessions, his clothing was fine and his food was good.

31.4.22.en: His table was abundant, his house resounded, his standing was awe-inspiring; he was rich and healthy, and everyone loved and honored him.

31.4.23.en: Splendid clothing, a healthy body, a full purse, and a life made pleasant with every good thing, without harm.

31.4.24.en: Rejoicing in his riches, proud of his garments, all of him splendid, luxurious and healthy, and he did not look upon the poor man.

31.4.25.en: Lazarus was at the door of this boaster, full of woes, and he saw the good things and did not murmur.

31.4.26.en: He only longed to be satisfied with the crumbs, and did not ask for the surplus that was there.

31.4.27.en: He did not desire clothing, nor riches, nor the foods that were abundant on the table.

31.4.28.en: He needed only the crumbs that the dogs eat; this is what nature requires, and this is what he longed for [7].

31.4.29.en: St. Jacob of Serugh It is a snare for those who devote their lives to it, and every fool falls into it [7].

31.4.30.en: When a man devotes his life to the love of the good things of the world, it corrupts his depths, and the good things of the world become evils to him.

31.4.31.en: * The good things of (the world) are in truth evils, and its evils (its afflictions) are also certainly good things.

31.4.32.en: All the good things of this world are full of death, and he who endures gathers life from its evils.

31.4.33.en: He who is at rest in it: torments are prepared and kept for him; and he who is tormented in it: he finds rest in the new world.

31.4.34.en: The Gospel of our Lord teaches men thus, and whoever wishes not to understand, that rests upon him.

31.4.35.en: He said plainly: He who finds himself destroys it, and he who destroys himself in the world finds it (Mt 10:39).

31.4.36.en: He who destroys himself is the one who toils, and is persecuted, and is crushed, and crucifies daily the passions and desires (Lk 9:23; Gal 5:24; 6:14).

31.4.37.en: And he dies every day for the hope of the world to come, and his life in the world which he does not love is a surplus.

31.4.38.en: And he who destroys himself here goes and finds a desirable place and a life of light without end.

31.4.39.en: And he finds his soul full of blessings in the great world, and in it the saying is fulfilled: he finds himself if he destroys it.

31.4.40.en: That one who boasts, and takes his ease, and sins, and swaggers (in his walk) admiring himself, in whom is the life of the world and all its pleasures, who loves riches, and whose soul is bound to possessions, who hates troubles and flees from torments, and finds himself in a pleasant life without annoyances, this one is destroyed, and makes the soul he has found guilty.

31.4.41.en: And he goes and inherits the sea of fire, like the rich man who received here all his good things, as it is said (Lk 16:25) [8].

31.4.42.en: St. Jacob of Serugh Blessed is the rich man who is found without blame, and does not go after gold [8].

31.4.43.en: There are blessed rich men, such as Abraham the father of the fathers, who was very rich (Gen 13:2). His wealth did not distract him from his attachment to God and the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, from his hospitality to strangers, and from making Sarah his wife a partner in serving them.

31.4.44.en: * It is necessary that gold follow you, not that you follow it. In truth gold is a good thing; surely God did not create anything evil. Do not be evil, and gold will become good.

31.4.45.en: Behold, I place gold in the hands of a godly person and of another who is unfaithful. If the unfaithful person takes it, the poor man is oppressed, those in authority are corrupted, the laws are broken, and social life is thrown into confusion. Why? Because the unfaithful man took the gold. And if the godly person takes it, the poor man is supported, the naked is clothed, the oppressed are set free, and the prisoners are rescued. How great is the good that the righteous person reaps from gold, and how many evils happen through the gold that the unfaithful man has taken!...

31.4.46.en: If you are unfaithful you will follow gold, and if you are godly gold will follow you. What does it mean that gold follows you? That you rule over it and are not its servant, because you possess it and it does not possess you [9].

31.4.47.en: St. Augustine Who is he, that we may call him blessed?

31.4.48.en: He does wonders in the midst of his people [9].

31.4.49.en: I rejoice in Your wonderful works, so that I forget even myself, and I delight in You alone. For what is better than You? In truth You are the great God, You do wonders in the body as in the soul, and You raise up from earthly man a son to Yourself, reflecting Your splendor upon him eternally.

31.4.50.en: * Wisdom works in everything; it accompanies all that is good. For how could it give good counsel unless justice were with it also, so that it might wrap itself in uprightness, and not fear death, and not draw back at any warning or fear, and not think it right to avoid the truth by any kind of flattery, nor avoid exile, knowing that the world is the homeland of the wise man? It does not fear want, knowing that nothing is lacking to the wise man, but the whole world with its riches is his. Who is greater than the man who knows not to be stirred at the thought of money, scorning wealth and holding it in contempt, like one who looks from a lofty foundation upon the desires of men? Men consider that one who acts thus is too exalted to be merely a man. It is said: "Who is he, that we may call him blessed? For he does wonders in his life" [9]. Surely one must marvel at him who scorns riches, looking to the fact that many care for them more than for their own safety [10].

31.5.0.en: St. Ambrose * He declares the wonders of God (Ps 1:9) who sees them accomplished not only openly in his body but also invisibly in his soul; indeed these wonders are more sublime and exalted. For men, being earthly, are led by what they see with the eye, and marvel the more that dead Lazarus rose in the body than that Paul the persecutor rose in the spirit (Jn 11; Acts 9). But the visible wonder calls the soul to enjoy the light, whereas through the invisible one a man passes on to understand it, and so speaks of all the wonders of God [11].

31.6.0.en: * To rejoice in the (wonderful) works of God is to forget even yourself, for you can delight in Him alone. For what is better than He? Do you not see this, that when you return to yourself you return to a sinful thing? "I will remember Your wonders of old" (Ps 11:77)... "You are the God that alone does wonders" (Ps 14:77). In truth You are the great God, You do wonders in the body as in the soul, You alone are the doer of them. The deaf hear, the blind see, the weak are healed, the dead rise, and the paralyzed are strengthened. But these wonders were accomplished at that time in the body. Let us look at those accomplished in the soul. Those who a little while ago were drunkards have become workers, those who a little while ago were idolaters have now become believers, those who formerly robbed others now offer gifts to the poor [12].

31.7.0.en: * "The heavens shall praise Your wonders, O Lord" (Ps 89:5)... For in every work of mercy toward lost souls, every work of justification of sinners, what do we praise but the wonderful works of God? You praise Him because the dead rise; praise Him the more because the lost have been saved. Yesterday, O man, you saw a whirlpool of drunkenness; now you see the beauty of self-control. Yesterday you saw a blasphemer of God; now you see him praising Him. Yesterday he was a slave of the creature; today he has become a worshiper of the Creator. Thus men have turned away from these dreadful conditions. Let them not look to their own merits. Let them become heavens and praise the wonders of Him who made them heavens" [13].

31.7.1.en: St. Augustine Who has been tried by it and found perfect? He may glory in it.

31.7.2.en: Who has been able to transgress and has not transgressed? And to do evil and has not done it? [10]

31.7.3.en: His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare his alms [11].

31.7.4.en: What commends a man for the Kingdom is not the amount of money, but his faithfulness in using it. Some were helped by money toward the salvation of their souls when they used it for the glory of God and the good of their brethren, being content with only what was necessary for themselves. Blessed, then, is that man who was able to sin and transgress the commandment because of money, but refrained from it through his fear of God. For his goods are established, because his conduct glorifies God.

31.7.5.en: * Show works of righteousness, for you are able to accomplish works according to your ability. Your fear of God and your obedience to Him are not shown in abstaining from works beyond your strength, but in those in which you are able to violate the Law, yet do not violate it [10]. If you give alms to the poor after having robbed them of what they had, it were better for you neither to take from them nor to give to them. Why do you defile your wealth, which in truth is your own, by adding to it money gained by injustice? Why do you offer a gift out of the injustice which you dared to present as an abomination, with the intention of showing mercy to another poor man? Be merciful to him against whom you have sinned. Show him kindness, and so you fulfill the duty of mercy together with justice. God has no fellowship with greed, and the Lord is not a companion of robbers and thieves. He did not leave the poor to us to feed them because He is unable to do this Himself, but He asks us to do it for our own good, as a fruit of mercy and justice [14].

31.8.0.en: 14 Remember that an evil eye is a great evil. 15 What has been created more wicked than the eye? Therefore it weeps from every person. 16 Wherever it glances, do not stretch out your hand to it, 17 and do not crowd it at the dish. 18 Understand what your neighbor has from what you have, and consider every matter. 19 Eat of what is set before you, as a man eats, and do not be greedy, lest you be hated. 20 Be the first to stop, out of good manners, and do not be insatiable, lest you be rebuked. 21 And when you sit among many, do not stretch out your hand before them. 22 How little suffices a well-bred man, and such a one does not gasp on his bed. 23 Sleeplessness, cholera and colic are for the gluttonous man. 24 The sleep of health is for the man moderate in his belly; he rises early and is master of himself. 25 And if you are forced to eat, withdraw from the midst of the company and rest. 26 Hear me, my son, and do not despise me, and in the end you will find my words true. 27 In all your works be diligent, and no sickness will overtake you. 28 He who is generous with food, lips bless him, and the testimony to his generosity is a true testimony. 29 He who is stingy with food, the city murmurs against him, and the testimony to his meanness is a sure testimony. 30 Do not play the hero in regard to wine, for wine has destroyed many. 31 The furnace tests the tempered iron, and wine tests the hearts of the proud in battle. 32 Wine is life to a man, if you drink it moderately. 33 What life is there for a man who has no wine? 34 What takes away life? Death. 35 Wine was created from the beginning to make men glad, not to make them drunk. 36 Wine is the gladness of the heart and the joy of the soul, to him who drinks of it in its time as much as suffices. 37 Drinking with gentleness is health to soul and body. 38 Excess in drinking wine is strife and contention. 39 Excess in drinking wine is bitterness to the soul. 40 Drunkenness stirs up the anger of the fool to his downfall, and lessens strength and multiplies wounds. 41 At a wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his merriment. 42 Do not speak to him words of reproach, and do not press him in demanding repayment.

31.8.1.en: Ben Sirach ties the conduct of man in every sphere to the wisdom that befits a man of God. It befits the believer, who bears the image of God and is an ambassador of the Lord Christ, to bear witness to the blessed, heaven-like life even in his eating and drinking, and indeed in his walking and the movements of his body. When a believer is invited to a table, it befits him to practice self-control and the restraint of the appetite for food, not for the sake of those who share the table with him, but for the sake of the soundness of his inner being. For while we care for the health of the body in sharing in banquets, it befits us to care for the health of the spirit.

31.8.2.en: He presents to us proper conduct at banquets, such as moderation in food and drink, commitment to godly conduct befitting the people of God, care in conversation during the banquet, and generosity in a spirit of wisdom.

31.8.3.en: The table is a wonderful school in which all, children and young people, adults and elders, learn how to enjoy the divine presence while they are at the table. We mention, by way of example, the following:

31.8.4.en: a. Not only does one begin to eat after prayer, but all feel that they are in the divine presence while they share in eating or in conversation during the meal. The godly man knows, during the meal, when to be silent and when to speak, and how to sanctify every breath of his life wherever he may be!

31.8.5.en: b. Banquets are a wonderful opportunity, not for a man to display his asceticism in food or his sharing it with others, but to express naturally what is in his depths of joy of the spirit and satisfaction with the divine presence.

31.8.6.en: c. The sanctification of time even in the moments of eating and drinking. I recall, for example, that at one of the church conferences between the Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Orthodox, during the lunch meal in Switzerland, I noticed that His Grace Anba Gregorios, Bishop of Coptic Studies, had turned his eyes for some minutes in a certain direction while silent. I asked him: "What are you thinking about?" He answered me: "I am looking at this small icon on the wall; it is Coptic art! Notice how the cheek of the Child Jesus clings to the cheek of St. Mary! St. Mary has become a unique divine throne upon which He sits and declares His love for mankind in the person of His mother according to the flesh!" And he told me the story of a British man who would not allow himself to sit on a chair in his house because Queen Victoria had sat on it one day. How great is St. Mary, in whose lap the King of kings sat?! This is what occupied the heart of His Grace Anba Gregorios while he was eating.

31.8.7.en: d. The sitting of children with their parents during a banquet or at home is counted a wonderful occasion for shaping their personalities, so that they may silently take from their parents a life of thanksgiving, of not being gluttonous, of not being preoccupied with food, and of consideration for others, so that they do not fill their plate more than they will eat! They realize that even in the midst of a banquet they are members of a holy congregation, which enjoys the earnest of heaven on every occasion.

31.8.8.en: e. Greed or gluttony is a great evil.

31.8.9.en: f. A man eats with good manners, and with deliberation, of what is set before him.

31.8.10.en: g. Let the believer be the first to stop eating.

31.8.11.en: h. The believer does not stretch out his hand to eat before the others.

31.8.12.en: i. Gluttony deprives a man of quiet sleep.

31.8.13.en: j. Not to exceed in drinking wine, lest a man perish.

31.8.14.en: k. Drunkenness stirs up anger and adds wounds to the soul.

31.8.15.en: l. At the wine banquet we do not rebuke anyone nor trouble him with our demands.

31.8.16.en: Are you sitting at the table of a great man? Do not be greedy, and do not say: "How much there is upon it!" [12].

31.8.17.en: It befits the wise man not to fix his eyes on the abundance of food or its variety, but on his inner satisfaction, the beauty of his depths, and the health of his spirit before God and heaven.

31.9.0.en: In the parable of "Lazarus and the rich man" (Lk 16:19-31), the Lord Christ linked the pride of the rich man with a life of luxury, especially his concern to hold banquets. St. Cyril the Great says: [Let us look at the pride of the rich man, who was arrogant because of things of no real value, for it is said: "He was clothed in purple and fine linen," that is, his concern was to adorn himself with beautiful clothing, and his garment was costly. He lived in unceasing banquets; this is what is meant by the words "fared sumptuously every day," besides the word "luxuriously," that is, wastefully... What was the result? It differs little from the forms of statues and paintings, for in truth the rich man was an object of admiration to those absorbed in the senses, but his heart was full of pride and haughtiness; he thought something of himself with arrogance, although there was nothing excellent in his mind, and he offered varied dishes because of his empty pride. His delight was in costly banquets, music and revelry; he had many cooks working to arouse gluttony with appetizing foods; the cupbearers wore beautiful clothes; he had male and female singers; he heard the voices of flatterers. Thus the rich man lived, therefore the disciple of Christ warns us, saying: "For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1 Jn 2:16). Meanwhile Lazarus suffered from sickness and poverty, cast out at the rich man's gate. The rich man dwelt in lofty halls and spacious, magnificent houses, while the poor man was cast outside, neglected, appearing as one who deserves nothing. Deprived of compassion and care, he found nothing to satisfy his hunger, and so he gathered the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. He also suffered from a grievous disease without remedy, yes, and the dogs licked his sores; and as it seems they did not harm him but comforted him and had compassion on him, for with their tongues they soothed his toils and removed what pained him and eased his sores. But the rich man was crueler than the beasts, for he neither had mercy on him nor comforted him, but was harsh [15].]

31.9.1.en: Remember that an evil eye is a great evil. What has been created more wicked than the eye?

31.10.0.en: Therefore it weeps for every face [16] [13].

31.10.1.en: The eye, which was created to support the spirit in enjoying spiritual insight, is not satisfied with the whole world if it is offered to it; what satisfies it is its meeting with God and its fellowship with Him, and its readiness to enjoy the heavenly table and the bread of angels.

31.10.2.en: Do not stretch out your hand to everything you see, and do not crowd anyone at a dish [14].

31.10.3.en: Taking part by accepting the invitation to the banquet does not mean ignoring self-control; it does not befit the believer to stretch out his hand to everything he looks at on the table.

31.11.0.en: Understand what your neighbor has [17] from what you have, and deliberate in every matter [15].

31.11.1.en: Eat of what is set before you, as a man eats, and do not devour it in a greedy manner, lest you be despised [16].

31.11.2.en: The believer takes care not to be a cause of distress to the host, confusing him with particular dishes that it may be hard for him to provide at that time.

31.11.3.en: Be the first to stop eating, out of good manners, and do not be greedy, lest you cause offense [17].

31.12.0.en: He points to the care to be taken in the manner of eating, for some have a disgusting way of eating, and this way often repels those who sit with them and arouses their revulsion, such as making a sound in the throat when gulping down water, and eating in a manner that betrays gluttony and a lack of cleanliness [18].

31.12.1.en: And when you sit at a table among many, do not stretch out your hand before them [18].

31.12.2.en: It befits the believer to stretch out his hand to the food after all have begun, and to finish before all.

31.13.0.en: * The mark of the moderate person is that he takes a small quantity when eating or drinking, but does this at a fitting time; so do not hurry to be the one who begins to eat, nor hesitate here and there to be the first to finish eating, so that you take on an attitude of indifference [19].

31.13.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * The mark of the man who has control of himself is that he takes a small quantity when he eats or drinks, but does so at a fitting time, and does not hurry as far as possible at the beginning of his eating, nor lag here and there. And he is the first to finish eating, and takes care not to display indifference. The Scripture says: "Be the first to stop eating, out of good manners... and when you sit at the table among many, do not stretch out your hand before them" (cf. Sir 31:19).

31.13.2.en: There is no need to say that it does not befit us not to lean forward in order to begin taking the food out of gluttony, just as it does not befit us to hold back too far and so confess, through our fault, that we have no control over ourselves.

31.14.0.en: At the same time we do not stand like those who guard their food, like animals that stand poised for their food, nor do we yield to pleasure through the many pleasures of food. It is a mark of self-control that we rise from the table before everyone and withdraw from it in a spirit of humility. It is said: "When the time has come, rise and do not delay; hasten to your house and do not loiter" (cf. Sir 31:11) [20].

31.14.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria How little suffices a well-bred man, and on his bed he does not breathe with difficulty [19].

31.14.2.en: To be content with eating little of what is set before one is not a commandment peculiar to monks; rather it befits all Christians to keep it.

31.14.3.en: Healthy sleep depends on moderation in food. He rises early with a good spirit.

31.14.4.en: But gluttony is accompanied by anxiety because of sleeplessness, and by vomiting and colic [20].

31.14.5.en: Healthy sleep depends on moderation in eating. St. John Chrysostom speaks to us of the vice of the desire for sumptuous food, showing that this pleasure quickly stops when the belly is filled, and sometimes before the feeling of satisfaction, for a man loses the attraction of this pleasure while the food is still in the mouth and has not yet been swallowed.

31.14.6.en: * Let us first examine the vice of pleasure concerning the sumptuous table, which is exceedingly attractive...

31.14.7.en: At the moment when a person begins to feel satisfied, the pleasure stops. Indeed sometimes it stops more quickly than the course of a flowing stream. And sometimes the pleasure does not remain until the food itself is swallowed, but stops while the food is between the teeth.

31.15.0.en: I am not speaking of the evils that follow this, nor of how dangerous the storm is that arises from the pleasures of the table. In truth, the person who abstains (from pleasure) not only feels comfortable, but feels light and more at ease than the one who lies in his bedchamber weighed down with a stuffed stomach. The Scripture says that healthy sleep depends on moderation in eating. Is there any need to summon sicknesses, indigestion, trials and waste? They come from such meals [21].

31.16.0.en: * We read: "The sleep of health is for the man moderate in his belly"; moderation in eating (cf. Sir 13:20). In whatever you keep the proper measure it is delightful, but he who exceeds the measure loses the pleasure [22].

31.16.1.en: St. John Chrysostom If you are stuffed with food, rise in the middle of the meal and stop eating [21].

31.16.2.en: This was a bad habit that was widespread among the Romans: when a person was invited to more than one banquet, he would rise after eating, go into the bath and vomit the food, and then prepare himself for the next banquet. Perhaps here he gives advice to the person who was compelled to eat too much under the pressure of the host.

31.16.3.en: Hear me, my son, and do not despise me, and you will realize that my words are important.

31.16.4.en: In all your works be ready, and no sickness will overtake you [22].

31.16.5.en: Ben Sirach fears that some may despise his words because he enters into the details of daily life, but he wishes the reader to arrive at a state of moderation in everything.

31.17.0.en: He who is generous in (offering) his food, lips bless him, and their testimony to his loftiness is trustworthy [23].

31.18.0.en: He who is stingy with food, the city murmurs against him, and their testimony to his stinginess is a true testimony [24].

31.18.1.en: While he rebukes the greedy guest, he urges the host to offer generously to his guest everything possible.

31.19.0.en: Do not prove your valor (by drinking) wine, for wine has destroyed many [25].

31.20.0.en: As the furnace tests the hardness of steel in the process of its tempering, so wine tests hearts in the fighting of the proud [26].

31.20.1.en: * Those are worthy of pity who withdraw from moderation in their gatherings, thinking that their life is happier when it turns to licentious drinking. Their life is nothing but festivals of licentious drunkenness, full of troubles (headache), marked by idleness and drinking and so on. You see some of them in truth half-drunk, stammering in speech with one another, putting garlands around their necks as though they were bottles (of drunkenness), and under the cover of sincere friendship each one spits wine upon the others... It was well said: "As the furnace tests the hard steel that is cast into it, so wine makes the heart proud" (cf. Sir 31:26) [23].

31.20.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Wine is like life to a man if you drink it moderately; what life is there for him who has no wine?

31.21.0.en: For it was created to make men glad [27].

31.22.0.en: Wine is the gladness of the heart and the joy of the soul, to him who drinks of it at the proper time and in moderation [28].

31.22.1.en: In the Old Testament wine pointed to pleasure and joy (Judg 9:13; Ps 104:15). So when the Virgin Lady came to the Lord Christ at the wedding of Cana of Galilee, she said to Him, "They have no wine," which means that joy had ceased from Israel, and this is what Ben Sirach meant here.

31.23.0.en: Excess in drinking wine is bitterness to the soul, and brings agitation, stumbling and falling [29].

31.23.1.en: * The Scripture says: "Do not be excessive in wine, for wine has shattered many" (cf. Sir 31:29). The Scythians and the Celts (an Indo-European race that dwelt in central and western Europe) and the people of the island of Iberia are occupied with drinking without limit, and they were all warlike peoples, and think that they are doing a noble and pleasant work. Let us, the peaceful people, celebrate our feasts and drink the cups of friendship without wine, so that we may be glad without committing sin [24].

31.24.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Drunkenness stirs up the anger of the fool to his hurt, and lessens his strength, and adds to his wounds [30].

31.24.1.en: * The Tragedian says: "Every man whom wine overcomes falls under his passions and is empty of reason, utters vain babble, and is compelled against his will to hear things that he said of his own will." Before this a warning was written by Wisdom: "Excessive drunkenness stirs up quarrels and causes much ruin" (cf. Sir 31:30) [25].

31.24.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria At the wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his revelry.

31.25.0.en: And do not utter a word of insult against him, and do not grieve him with demands that you make of him [31].

31.25.1.en: In the discourse of Pope Gregory (the Great) on pastoral care, he stresses the obligation to act at the right moment. He calls us to act without fear but in a spirit of wisdom [26].

31.25.2.en: * Since God knows that drinking wine in moderation is healthy and increases discernment, while he who gulps it down without measure engenders vices (cf. Sir 31:30-42), He gave us this creature. He left to mankind the freedom and the possibility of using it abundantly, so that even by using a small quantity it might be a lesson in sobriety, and the condition of human nature bears the error and destruction of its misuse and the commission of the crime of drunkenness. Noah became drunk and reeling because of wine, and fell into a deep sleep (Gen 9:21). In this way he who had acquired glory through the Flood came into shame through wine. Nevertheless the Lord preserved the good qualities in wine by its nature, so that He made its fruit contribute to our salvation, and caused us to receive the forgiveness of sins by its use (in the Divine Liturgy) [27].

31.25.3.en: St. Ambrose * Let us keep far, far away from jesting, for it is the beginning of abuse, by which fierce quarrels develop, and family enmities, and the rising up of enemies. We believe that arrogance accompanies drunkenness... The Scripture says: "At the wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor" [28].

31.25.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Inspired by Sirach 31

31.26.s.en: I long to enjoy the heavenly table!

31.26.0.en: * Grant me, O Lord, faithfulness in the little over which You have set me, so that You may set me over the much that You are preparing for me.

31.26.1.en: By Your wisdom I trade with the talents here, that I may enjoy the glories in eternity.

31.26.2.en: Take away from me every attachment to temporal wealth, so that I may enjoy Your peace in my waking as in my sleep.

31.26.3.en: May I enjoy health of spirit as health of body.

31.26.4.en: I will stretch out my hand to give, not to take.

31.26.5.en: I will manage what I have with wisdom, so that nothing enslaves me.

31.26.6.en: I will not be a captive to grief nor to pain, but I will enjoy the glory of the children of God.

31.26.7.en: Instead of the luxurious life, I put on Your splendid righteousness.

31.26.8.en: I will not devote my heart to passing temporal things, but to You, O Eternal One.

31.26.9.en: * You promised me that You go up to prepare a place for me.

31.26.10.en: What place do You prepare for me except that You make me ready to rest in Your bosom?!

31.26.11.en: Queen Esther was not pleased to sit at the king's table, but enjoyed the table of heaven!

31.26.12.en: For the sake of love I share with my brethren, without desire for eating or drinking.

31.26.13.en: When I begin to pray at the table, I ask that You not deprive me of the bread of angels.

31.26.14.en: I want to be drunk with Your divine love, that my soul may rejoice.

31.26.15.en: The food of the world, if it increases a little, confuses my soul and body.

31.26.16.en: But the food of heaven increases my hunger and thirst for You, O Satisfier of souls!
